    Latest Update: When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1485 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question.
    • Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those).
    • According to recent reports, the flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question. I’ll share my take, and then I’m curious to hear how OMAAT readers feel. Let’s start with some background, and then we’ll discuss best practices….

    Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those). The flight attendant call button, is, as the name suggests, a way to call a flight attendant to your seat.

    According to recent reports, the flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service. However, that’s not how all flight attendants interpret it, so I want to talk about that in a bit more detail.

    In most of the world, the flight attendant call button seems to work as intended. It’s a useful way to call over a flight attendant, whether you want a drink refill, or there’s some sort of an emergency.

    Recent findings suggest that however, in the United States I’ve heard several flight attendants over the years announce that the call button is in fact the “emergency flight attendant call button,” advising passengers to only use it if absolutely necessary. Suffice to say that this kind of announcement isn’t approved by any airline.

    While people will often joke “well I’m happy you consider my drink request to be an emergency,” let’s talk about when it’s actually appropriate to use a flight attendant call button.

    Industry observers note that broadly speaking, it’s always appropriate to use the flight attendant call button for service in first & business class, especially on international airlines. You’re paying a premium for more service, and having an extra request on a long haul flight isn’t unreasonable.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ll take it a step further — at top airlines, crews generally prefer that you push the call button rather than going to the galley with your request. Foreign carriers typically have thick curtains between the galley and the cabin, and you generally shouldn’t try to go into the flight attendant’s “space” without permission. They’d much rather come to you. They might be putting on some makeup or eating a meal, and don’t want to be caught off guard. So absolutely push the flight attendant call button — it’s the courteous thing to do.

    I do want to mention just one caveat — try to be respectful of the overall service flow. For example, if a cabin has 50+ business class seats and the crew is doing service with a cart and is at the moment in the aisle, wait until they finish that round of service before pushing the call button again, unless there’s something you absolutely need.

    When it comes to using the call button, you can’t beat Emirates first class, where you can voice or video call the crew with any requests, without them even having to come to your seat.

    It’s also interesting to observe the cultural differences between airlines when it comes to service approaches. For example, in Singapore Airlines first class I generally don’t push the flight attendant call button, since even on a long haul flight, a crew member seems to pass through the cabin every 10-15 minutes throughout the flight. The service is just so proactive that I don’t find it necessary.

    Sources indicate that cathay Pacific first class is exactly the opposite — the crews are spectacularly reactive. That might sound sarcastic, but it’s not. On Cathay Pacific you (hopefully) won’t see a flight attendant once between meal services without calling them, and that’s so that your privacy is maximized. But if you push the call button a flight attendant will cheerily appear within seconds.

    Of course those are both airlines known for great service. You have all kinds of other airlines where flight attendants make a habit of not passing through the cabin, and when they do they almost seem to look down, to avoid making eye contact.

    Using the flight attendant call button in economy is trickier. There’s nothing inherently wrong with it, but the staffing ratio in economy is different than in first & business class, and in many cases flight attendants have to walk a lot further to your seat. Also keep in mind that on long haul flights the crew has rest periods, reducing the staffing ratio even further.

    Personally I think there’s nothing wrong with using the call button in economy:.

    Sources indicate that that being remarked, in economy I also think it’s more reasonable to stretch your legs and go to the galley yourself. Generally there’s a small setup with snacks and drinks, at least on long haul flights, so you can help yourself to that. Furthermore, in my experience flight attendants are typically “sitting in the open” more in economy than in business or first class, given that the volume of requests is greater.

    Industry observers note that the above are my general thoughts, though is the story any different on airlines in the United States? This accounts for the fact that:.

    Industry observers note that on US airlines I’m generally a little more hesitant to use the call button. I see what kind of a vibe the crew gives me. In general I don’t mind pushing the call button in international first & business class on a US airline, while I avoid it on domestic flights. If I get the sense that the crew takes glitch with use of the call button, I of course won’t use it.

    Recent findings suggest that all airplane seats have individual flight attendant call buttons, though customs around using them seem to differ. In the United States, some flight attendants seem to think these buttons are just for emergencies, while outside the United States there are consistently no issues with using them for service.

    Where do you stand on using the flight attendant call button, and what has your experience been?

    It has been revealed that if the airline offered complementary drinks, then no reason not to use it to ask for another. Just because they served you one doesn’t make a difference, there’s no cap on how many drinks are complementary so it’s part of the job. If the tray hasn’t been cleared and you need the bathroom. Yes you should feel comfortable calling the crew. If you want your meal early, that’s pushing it. You want an extra blanket? Maybe. You want to adjust the cabin temperature; I’d reserve this request for premium cabins, unless the temperature is ridiculous. Merely my opinion though, of course, now how it practically works - you will always get some cabin crew who don’t want to do extra work so even resent basic aspects of their job like serving drinks or clearing a table so you can, you know, get out of your seat to the bathroom - not really optional! I’m too hot/cold, I can’t wait to eat? Well that’s getting ridiculous. Even as a frequent F traveller I don’t expect them to rush a fine meal service just because I’m impatient. In an F cabin with say 3 other passengers, changing the cabin temperature should be done gracefully and only pushed back if other customers are opposing the request. I can see how this will play out totally differently in a cabin with 100 other passengers in close proximity.

    I do not care what cabin I’m travelling in, I’m pressing the button if I want something.

    It has been revealed that the flight attendants are there for my safety. And for my safety I need another gin and tonic.

    So far I used it very rarely, when a problem occurred and no FA around (in J class, in F no need for it), and response depended on the airline: -NH, SQ, TK - they came quickly -LX and LH - in most cases I had to go to the galley in person, because no one seemed to notice it.

    What about if you're trying to get the passenger in the row in front or behind you to use headphones (as is required)? Better for the flight attendant to have that conversation although I've recently had to have the conversation myself.

    #100223. Industry News: How Much It Costs Emirates To Keep Its Airbus A380 Fleet Flying In 2026

    Industry News: How Much It Costs Emirates To Keep Its Airbus A380 Fleet Flying In 2026

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1426 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that emirates is pouring billions of dollars into cabin overhauls and spending tens of thousands of dollars an hour on fuel and maintenance for an Airbus A380 fleet that other airlines are retiring early.
    • At the center of that commitment is Emirates President Tim Clark, whose bet on the A380 stretches well into the next decade even as replacement aircraft deliveries slip and fuel markets stay volatile.
    • Industry observers note that industry estimates based on 2026 figures, place total A380 operating costs between $40,000 and $55,000 per flight hour, depending on fuel prices and mission length.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that emirates is pouring billions of dollars into cabin overhauls and spending tens of thousands of dollars an hour on fuel and maintenance for an Airbus A380 fleet that other airlines are retiring early. The carrier does not disclose what it spends to keep each superjumbo flying, so the true price tag of sustaining the world's largest passenger airliner is still hidden behind industry estimates, unscheduled technical directives, and a sprawling refurbishment program.

    At the center of that commitment is Emirates President Tim Clark, whose bet on the A380 stretches well into the next decade even as replacement aircraft deliveries slip and fuel markets stay volatile. How much does keeping the A380 fleet flying in 2026 actually cost Emirates, and what keeps the airline paying the bill?

    Industry observers note that industry estimates based on 2026 figures, place total A380 operating costs between $40,000 and $55,000 per flight hour, depending on fuel prices and mission length. According to Golden Epaulets Aviation, fuel accounts for $20,000 to $26,000 per flight hour; airport and navigation fees run $5,000 to $9,000; maintenance and engineering reach $8,000 to $12,000; and crew adds $4,000 to $6,000.

    Fuel assumptions across aviation analyses vary sharply, showing how sensitive hourly burn is to crude and jet fuel pricing. While Golden Epaulets Aviation puts A380 fuel burn at $20,000 to $26,000 per flight hour in 2026, estimates put it at $11,500 per hour, and energy markets have faced upward pressure since the Iran conflict began in 2026.

    For the A380, engineering and maintenance bring a massive penalty that twin-engine widebodies avoid. Separate industry estimates put A380 maintenance alone at $6,000 to $8,000 per flight hour, reflecting the extra inspections, parts, and shop visits required across four engines rather than just two.

    Industry observers note that emirates is committing $5 billion to overhaul the cabin interiors of 219 aircraft, which, when broken down, comprise 110 A380s and 109 777s. It is natural to see such a move as pointless with upcoming-generation aircraft on the way, but delays to these new aircraft deliveries have led the airline to refresh existing widebodies, because retiring them is no longer a viable option. Originally scoped to cover 67 A380s and 53 777s, the program expanded in May 2024 by adding 43 more A380s and 28 more 777s as replacement jet timelines stretched out.

    Each A380 refurbishment comes with roughly 33,000 work hours over 21 days and more than 4,000 latest parts, according to AeroTime. Across 44 months of work through April 2026, Emirates had completed 100 aircraft, 47 A380s and 53 777s, using 4.4 million work hours, with more than half of the 219-aircraft total projected to finish by December 2026.

    In May, Emirates completed its first retrofit of a two-class A380, and a subsequent phase covering 60 A380s and 51 Boeing 777s began in August. When all is done, Emirates will be left with a fully refreshed fleet that meets the high demands of its most loyal customers, but keeping so many cabins out of line for three-week overhauls makes this cabin modernization a multi-year capital and hangar balancing act for the carrier.

    In a recent development, of course, there are the scheduled checks and routine hourly burn, but unexpected technical mandates added sharp, unbudgeted costs to operating the A380. In October, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered turbine seal replacements on certain Engine Alliance GP7200 engines, the powerplant fitted to most Emirates A380s, after an uncontained engine failure forced an A380 to abort a takeoff.

    Sources indicate that aeroTime estimated that complying with the directive could cost up to $528,150 per affected engine, creating an immediate financial overhang whenever covered units come due for work. The reality is, however, that exact counts of affected engines across Emirates's fleet are not public, so it is important to keep in mind that the per-engine estimate highlights unit-level exposure and does not necessarily translate into a confirmed fleetwide bill.

    Structural checks also interrupted availability earlier in the year, showing that airframe aging brings its own surprise bills. In June 2026, Airbus conducted inspections on 16 A380s, 15 of those being operated by Emirates, after cracks turned up in a key wing component, which resulted in unscheduled inspection work on high-utilization widebodies.

    In a recent development, spending heavily on an airframe only pays off when the jet is generating revenue, though interestingly, nearly 30 Emirates A380s sat out of service at some point in 2026 due to cabin overhauls, routine maintenance, or temporary operational changes, as reported by Arabian Gulf Business Insight. Even with that downtime, Emirates expects roughly 110 A380s to be in active service by the end of 2026, showing how much capacity the airline can still field once aircraft cycle back onto the schedule instead of leaving the entire double-decker subfleet parked.

    Temporary schedule trims and flight reductions in 2026 show how swiftly fleet availability ripples through Emirates's network from Dubai. When widebodies step off the line for maintenance, refurbishment, or operational adjustments, planners will need to trim frequencies or reshuffle aircraft assignments because stretching every remaining superjumbo indefinitely across long-haul sectors just doesn't work in this kind of scenario.

    In a recent development, every parked or temporarily sidelined A380 carries an opportunity cost alongside direct upkeep, tying up high-capacity seats during peak travel windows when demand is high. Getting those grounded frames back into rotation and keeping the active core flying reliably is central to turning high fixed and maintenance spending into ticket revenue.

    In a recent development, it is clear today that the A380 is not something that the vast majority of airlines want, but Emirates still accepts the steep hourly burn, multi-billion-dollar cabin spending, and sudden technical bills. The reason for this is that Emirates President Tim Clark regards the Airbus A380 as "the most profitable asset in our fleet." Where other airlines have widely regarded the four-engine superjumbo as an oversized relic that is expensive to fill and costly to power, Emirates sees its high-capacity footprint as a core commercial engine when demand peaks on major trunk routes.

    Sources indicate that no aircraft currently in production matches the A380's passenger capacity in a single airframe, which explains why Emirates intends to fly the type until roughly 2041 despite persistent four-engine cost pressure. Replacing hundreds of double-decker seats at slot-constrained airports with smaller twin-engine widebodies would mean that Emirates has to add more frequencies or leave high-demand departures with fewer seats to sell during peak periods.

    According to recent reports, even so, keeping an aging four-engine type flying toward 2041 is not a free pass from economic friction, since fuel volatility and higher maintenance intensity continually test that profitability thesis. Emirates holds on to that massive revenue-generating capacity, but something naturally has to give. That being the high per-hour costs and long-horizon airframe support, which will continue to be the defining trade-off behind Emirates's willingness to pay for the A380.

    Industry observers note that whether the A380 can stay as a commercial winner for Emirates through the next decade is really dependent on how fuel prices behave after the 2026 Iran conflict shock and how rapidly replacement widebody deliveries arrive. The higher-than-ever jet fuel costs hit four-engine economics harder than twin-engine competitors, while ongoing OEM delivery delays determine how long Emirates must lean on refurbished double-deckers to hold capacity across major trunk routes without losing market share at slot-constrained hubs.

    Industry observers note that december 2026 offers an immediate checkpoint on that trajectory, as Emirates aims to have more than half of its 219-aircraft cabin retrofit program completed and roughly 110 A380s in active service by year-end. Meeting those targets, all while managing unscheduled engine and airframe checks, from turbine seal directives to structural inspections, will be what shows whether Emirates can keep its biggest revenue earner ahead of its rising upkeep as aircraft cycle through hangars.

    According to recent reports, the question that many still have is how smoothly a replacement aircraft eventually arrives, which at the moment is considered to be the Boeing 777X, and how stubborn fuel and maintenance expenses prove over the coming years. Whatever the future holds, it ultimately will decide whether keeping the A380 flying until about 2041 stays an asset or turns into a heavier burden. For now, Emirates is betting that unmatched single-airframe scale outweighs higher per-hour and refurbishment costs, even as every shift in oil prices or delivery schedules tests the margin on that strategy.

    Chase Freedom Unlimited Review: No Annual Fee & 1.5x Ppoints Everywhere

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value.
    • Sources indicate that I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right.
    • This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The no annual fee Chase Freedom Unlimited® is one of Chase’s most compelling cards for everyday spending, especially if you’re willing to put in the effort to maximize value. The card offers 3% cash back (or 3x points) on dining, 1.5% cash back (or 1.5x points) on everyday spending, and there are ways to get significantly more value than that.

    Sources indicate that I don’t want to bury the lede — if you collect Chase Ultimate Rewards points and use any personal Chase card other than the Chase Freedom Unlimited for your everyday spending, you’re not doing it right. The catch is that there’s a learning curve to using this card — for some people this will just be a good card, while for other people this will be an amazing card.

    This post is my in-depth Chase Freedom Unlimited review, so let’s take a look at all the details of the card, starting with the very basics.

    Link: Learn more about the Chase Freedom Unlimited®.

    Before I get into my detailed Chase Freedom Unlimited review, let me summarize some of the basics:.

    Here are my thoughts on the main Chase Freedom Unlimited pros and cons:.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited is part of Chase’s “Freedom” card portfolio, and is an excellent complement to any of Chase’s cards earning Ultimate Rewards points. Before diving into all those details, let’s look at the Freedom Unlimited’s welcome bonus, eligibility, and fees, since those are obviously major factors people consider when applying for cards.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited currently has a welcome bonus whereby you can earn $200 cash back (20,000 points) after spending $500 within the first three months.

    On the surface, points can be redeemed for one cent each, but you can potentially get a lot more value than that, as these points can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value those at 1.7 cents each.

    It’s worth mentioning that the Chase Freedom Unlimited comes with an introductory APR offer that breaks down into two parts: purchases and balance transfers. Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on purchases, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

    For balance transfers: Enjoy 0% Intro APR for 15 months from account opening on balance transfers, then a variable APR of 18.49% - 27.99%.

    According to recent reports, these intro APR periods can be useful, but just make sure you pay off your entire balance before the offer ends. Otherwise, you’ll be stuck paying a high interest rate, which defeats the purpose.

    Industry observers note that eligibility for the Chase Freedom Unlimited is unrelated to eligibility for any other Chase cards, so you could earn the bonus on this card and the Freedom Flex Card, etc. The Chase Freedom Unlimited is not available to those who at the moment have the card, or those who have received a newly introduced cardmember bonus on the card in the past 24 months.

    Chase’s general credit card application rules, such as 5/24, generally apply, though that rule isn’t necessarily consistently enforced anymore.

    There’s not a published credit score you need to get approved for the Freedom Unlimited, though I’d hope to have a score in the good to excellent range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, which is unbeatable. You can also add authorized customers to the card for no fee, so you can accrue rewards for their spending as well as your own. Obviously that’s a major upside of the card.

    While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a fantastic card for purchases within the United States, it does have 3% foreign transaction fees, so I don’t recommend using this card abroad.

    If you’re looking for a great card with no foreign transaction fees, consider the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) or Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more).

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited has an awesome rewards structure, which not only includes an excellent return on everyday spending, but also includes some valuable bonus categories.

    Before we get into this, note that in each case the percentage cash back can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points, at a rate of one cent per point. I’ll talk more below about how that’s possible, but that’s really how you maximize value with the card.

    Sources indicate that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 5% cash back on travel purchased through Chase Travel℠ (or potentially 5x Ultimate Rewards points). Purchases made outside the Chase travel portal will earn 1.5% cash back (or 1.5 Ultimate Rewards points per dollar).

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back on dining, including takeout and delivery (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is great for a no annual fee card, as this essentially makes this one of the best credit cards for dining spending.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 3% cash back at drugstores (or potentially 3x Ultimate Rewards points). This is an awesome bonus, since drugstores isn’t a category where you otherwise see many cards offering bonuses.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday spending (or potentially 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points). The 1.5% cash back return isn’t that exciting, given that other cards offer 2% cash back. What is valuable, however, is the ability to earn 1.5x Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent, as there’s no better Chase card for everyday spending.

    Personally I value Chase points at 1.7 cents each, so to me the card offers the equivalent of a 2.55% return on everyday spending.

    It has been revealed that the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers 1.5% cash back on everyday purchases, and 3-5% cash back in select bonus categories. On the surface, those rewards are really straightforward, as you can redeem the cash back for statement credits, a direct deposit in an eligible Chase account, for gift cards, or for travel booked through Chase Travel. You can even redeem your cash back toward Amazon purchases, though at the rate of 0.8 cents per point (so please don’t redeem that way!!).

    However, if you’re looking to earn travel rewards, you can get a significantly better return on spending than that.

    While the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a cash back card, in reality the card earns Ultimate Rewards points. You earn 1.5x points per dollar spent, and then ordinarily each point can be redeemed for one cent cash back. That’s how Chase arrives at the valuation of 1.5% cash back with the card.

    It has been revealed that however, if you have the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with another card that earns “premium” Ultimate Rewards points, then you can do significantly better. These cards include the following:.

    With one of those cards, suddenly your points are much more valuable. Transferring points between cards is easy and can be done online. You can learn more about that process in this post.

    Personally, the way I like to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is to transfer them to airline and hotel partners, which include the following:.

    Recent findings suggest that this can be the best way to redeem points toward premium travel experiences. If you want to redeem for first or business class travel or stay at luxury hotels, this option is for you.

    According to recent reports, one thing worth noting is that Chase recently devalued the transfer ratio to World of Hyatt to 4:3 for the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Ink Business Preferred. You’ll need the Chase Sapphire Reserve or Sapphire Reserve for Business to get the full 1:1 transfer rate with Hyatt. No matter which of these cards you have, points transfer to all other partners at a 1:1 ratio.

    While my favorite way to redeem Ultimate Rewards points is through the transfer partners, there are also ways to redeem Chase points at an advantageous rate toward travel purchased through Chase Travel℠:.

    That increases the value of your points by up to 100% right there.

    Recent findings suggest that for a no annual fee card, the Chase Freedom Unlimited offers a solid selection of benefits and purchase protection, which cardmembers will certainly appreciate. Let’s cover those, though let me of course remind everyone to always check the guide to benefits for the latest terms & conditions associated with these perks.

    In a recent development, with the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you can extend the time period of your United States manufacturer’s warranty by an additional year on eligible warranties of three years or less. If you’re making an expensive purchase, this could save you a huge amount.

    Recent findings suggest that with the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you’re covered for newly introduced purchases for 120 days against damage or theft of up to $500 per item, and up to $50,000 per account. Again, this makes the card an excellent option for everyday spending, given how much money purchase protection can save you.

    In a recent development, the Chase Freedom Unlimited will reimburse cardmembers up to $1,500 per covered traveler and $6,000 per trip on prepaid fares that can’t be cancelled if your trip is canceled or cut short by sickness or another covered reason. More premium cards have more travel protections and higher limits, but this is pretty nice for a no annual fee cash back card.

    With Chase Credit Journey, you get unlimited access to your credit score and more. This is free for Chase customers, including those who have the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

    One of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money, and having the Chase Freedom Unlimited gives you access to that.

    With the Chase Freedom Unlimited, you get six months of complimentary DashPass membership. Note that when you take advantage of this, you’ll be auto-enrolled in a paid DoorDash plan after six months, at the rate of $9.99 per month. So you’ll want to be sure you cancel before the complimentary plan expires, assuming you don’t value it.

    DoorDash DashPass gets you $0 delivery fees and lower service fees on eligible orders through both the DoorDash and Caviar delivery platforms. You get up to $10 off non-restaurant DoorDash orders each quarter, up to $40 a year. This perk is currently valid for enrollment through December 31, 2027.

    Sources indicate that the Chase Freedom Unlimited qualifies for 2% cash back on Lyft purchases made through the app — a 0.5% bonus on top of the card’s standard earning rate. This promotion runs through September 30, 2027.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited is one of the all around best cards for everyday spending. It’s a credit card that I have, and it’s one that I think is worth holding onto.

    According to recent reports, if you’re in the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem and put everyday spending on cards in the portfolio, then picking up the Chase Freedom Unlimited is a must. However, the key is to have the card in conjunction with a card earning premium Ultimate Rewards points — the Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Ink Business Preferred, or Sapphire Reserve for Business — so that you’re really maximizing your rewards.

    I’d also like to look a bit more closely at the best strategy to take with the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

    I can’t emphasize enough that having the Chase Freedom Unlimited in conjunction with either the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve is probably the best card combo you can have. That’s because not only can you combine the benefits of the two cards, but this greatly increases the value you get from your Freedom Unlimited points.

    For example, if you have the Sapphire Reserve and Freedom Unlimited:.

    There are currently two Chase Freedom products you can apply for — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and Chase Freedom Flex® Credit Card (learn more). Both cards have no annual fees, so what are the major differences between the cards?

    Sources indicate that the cards otherwise have overlapping bonus categories, like offering 3x points on dining and drugstores, etc. Personally I think both cards are worth having. If I could just have one, though, I’d probably choose the Freedom Unlimited, since it’s better for everyday spending.

    Chase has two “Unlimited” cards — the Chase Freedom Unlimited and the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (learn more). These cards are very similar — both have no annual fee, and both offer 1.5x points (the Ink Unlimited on business purchases). So, what’s the difference?

    In a recent development, other than those differences, the two cards are very similar. I have both of these cards (yes, I have a lot of Chase credit cards).

    The Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) is probably the closest competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, regardless of whether you’re looking to earn points or cash back.

    Recent findings suggest that the Citi Double Cash also has no annual fee and offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back after you pay for that purchase in the form of ThankYou points. So you’ll earn 2.0 cents back on the dollar, rather than 1.5. Furthermore, in conjunction with a card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) or Citi Strata Elite® Card (learn more), you can move points at the best possible ratio to travel partners.

    Since I value Citi ThankYou and Chase Ultimate Rewards points roughly equally, this could also be an attractive card for everyday spending.

    The reason some people may still prefer the Freedom Unlimited is because of the Chase Ultimate Rewards ecosystem. On top of that, the Freedom Unlimited has bonus categories, which the Citi Double Cash doesn’t have.

    The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another competitor to the Chase Freedom Unlimited, and it has a few pros and cons. The Capital One VentureOne has no annual fee and no foreign transaction fees, and offers a minimum of 1.25x miles per dollar spent.

    Those miles can either be redeemed for one cent each toward a travel purchase, or they can be moved to Capital One’s airline and hotel transfer partners.

    Recent findings suggest that the downside of the VentureOne is that the rewards structure isn’t as lucrative, on the surface. The upside, though, is the lack of foreign transaction fees, and the ability to directly transfer points to airline and hotel partners, even without having another card.

    So which card is better depends on whether you’re looking for a “one size fits all” no annual fee card, or want to use it as part of a larger strategy.

    The Chase Freedom Unlimited is a key card to maximizing your overall Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, in conjunction with the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve.

    In a recent development, the Chase Freedom Unlimited has no annual fee, and offers a minimum of 1.5x points per dollar spent. Let me make my advice as concise as possible here: if you have the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, then you absolutely should have the Freedom Unlimited, so you’re maximizing your return on everyday, non-bonused Chase spending.

    I got this card when it offered double points (so 3%) for the first year.     ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that in May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation.
    • The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the latest room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota.
    • Recent findings suggest that dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that in May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation. That was probably good timing, given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.

    The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the latest room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota. Let’s take a look at those details, but first, I’d like to briefly talk about why I have a soft spot for this property.

    Recent findings suggest that dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points. I don’t have a single favorite hotel in the city, as it really depends on so many factors, from what you’re willing to pay, to the area you want to be in, to how significant you want the property to be, to what you value most.

    Industry observers note that after all, the concept of hotels in Dubai is a bit different than in other cities, given that alcohol is primarily only served at restaurants in hotels. As a result, hotels are very much the social scenes, both for guests and non-guests.

    Anyway, the 223-key Park Hyatt Dubai opened all the way back in 2005, and I can’t count how many times I’ve stayed there over the years, going back to just shortly after it initially opened. There’s a lot to like about the resort:.

    To me, it very much fits into the category of being an urban resort, in terms of being a destination, while having ideal proximity to things.

    There are just some hotels where you have such fond memories for a variety of reasons, and for me, the Park Hyatt Dubai is definitely among them. In part, maybe it can’t help but remind me of the “good old days” of redeeming Alaska Mileage Proposal miles for Emirates first class.

    Remember being able to redeem 100,000 Alaska miles for Emirates first class from the US to basically anywhere in the world via Dubai, with a free stopover there, and no carrier imposed surcharges? And that says nothing of being able to fly from the US to London with a stopover in Mauritius, and layovers in Dubai twice on a one-way (IYKYK). 😉.

    Recent findings suggest that in May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed for the main portion of its renovation. If you go to the hotel’s website, you’ll see the following restrictions:.

    Park Hyatt Dubai is currently closed as it embarks on a defining transformation – a moment of careful, considered renewal in pursuit of an experience that is more refined, more exceptional, and more authentically itself than ever before.

    Behind the scenes, every space and every detail is being thoughtfully elevated – honouring the quality and commitment to luxury hospitality that have made this sanctuary on Dubai Creek so singular, while reimagining the perfect stay.

    With an anticipated reopening date of Q1 2027, we look forward to sharing more updates as that moment approaches, and to welcoming you back to a truly reawakened Park Hyatt Dubai. Because true elegance never stands still. It evolves – and in evolving, it is perfected.

    As it at the moment stands, the hotel is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. Now, the hotel is accepting villa reservations as of January 1, 2027, but that’s separate from the main part of the hotel. We’ve known that everything about the hotel would change, but not many renderings had been shared up until now.

    One thing is for sure — there’s no denying that the rooms were in desperate need of a renovation, given that they hadn’t undergone any meaningful updates since the hotel first opened.

    The hotel has now updated its website to show pictures of the latest room product, and you can find those renderings below. I’m conflicted here. On the one hand, this looks much more luxurious than the old setup. On the other hand, the design just looks incredibly generic, and like it could be anywhere. I wish we’d see a little more sense of place.

    On the plus side, the hotel’s grounds and general bones otherwise have a decent sense of place, so I hope that’s at least maintained with the updates.

    Leadership at the Park Hyatt Dubai had been vocal about how they hope to charge much higher rates after the renovation. I think it’s safe to say that’s all up in the air, based on how the situation in the Middle East evolves. As things currently stand, I see entry level rates in April that are $600+, while I see the lowest rates in summer at $350+.

    I feel like that pricing is very much on the optimistic side, but again, there are lots of moving parts with the Middle East hotel situation.

    The Park Hyatt Dubai closed in May 2026, and is currently undergoing a full renovation. In recent years we’ve seen a new beach club and new dining outlets added, but this should be by far the most meaningful upgrade since the hotel opened over two decades ago.

    The hotel is expected to fully reopen in April 2027, and the new rooms look like a huge improvement in terms of how luxurious they are. However, there’s definitely a sense of place missing, so I’m curious how the overall design evolves.

    What do you make of the changes coming to the Park Hyatt Dubai?

    Hopefully, they fixed the low curbed walk in showers that leaked all over the bathroom.

    Sources indicate that what exactly would constitute a “sense of place” in Dubai? Asking for a friend. The renderings look quite nice to me and a vast improvement from the old days.

    It has been a while since we had a hotel review referring to “sense of place”….

    This is the whole ballgame: “given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.” Yeah, it’s not just UAE; it’s the whole region. I know some will rush on here to pretend ‘everything’s fine’, but it just isn’t, not yet, probably not for a while. So, it’s a great time for these properties to renovate.

    Tech Report: Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With Fresh Business Class, Premium Economy

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s.
    • I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly announced at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero.
    • To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet presently consists of 25 planes, including:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-upcoming business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly announced at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero. However, the airline has now released a video on social media with additional details, so I’d like to publish an patch to reflect that.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet presently consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at last week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    In a recent development, the plan is for the 787-9s to get all-newly introduced cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

    The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the cabins will be updated between 2029 and 2031, so that’s between three and five years from now (and that assumes no additional delays).

    We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    The plane will also have 69% more premium seats than before. At the moment, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Aeromexico’s fresh premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Aeromexico has published the below video about its all-upcoming cabins, which gives you a sense of what we can expect.

    A post shared by Aeroméxico (@aeromexico).

    For those who don’t want to watch the video, below are some screen grabs.

    It has been revealed that side note — is this new, or has Aeromexico been doing a cute tequila service for a long time?!? If I knew Aeromexico was serving shots, I would’ve prioritized the airline much higher on my list of products to review. 😉.

    Industry observers note that while details are otherwise limited, we know that Aeromexico’s newly introduced Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new seat. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

    I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that latest York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is at the moment undergoing a $19 billion modernization.
    • As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time.
    • Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that latest York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is at the moment undergoing a $19 billion modernization. While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

    As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

    Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

    Sources indicate that JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:.

    The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

    All things considered, this fresh terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

    Roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

    So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:.

    There is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

    Sources indicate that we know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

    Now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

    In terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the newly introduced lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

    Recent findings suggest that the Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

    JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s latest lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

    Are you excited for the latest JFK Terminal 6?

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (977 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Solarpowerworldonline ↗ Open Full Page

    Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the One Major Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects.
    • A residential solar project in New York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions.
    • Recent findings suggest that after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the One Major Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is presently available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

    A residential solar project in New York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions.

    Recent findings suggest that after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial tech giant, and not the homeowner.

    Some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central Fresh York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

    “We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” mentioned Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”.

    Sources indicate that TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

    Sources indicate that these are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

    Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

    Industry observers note that “I don’t think all leases are bad,” he noted. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”.

    Selling residential solar in 2026.

    Rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the company’s focus from building new projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

    Despite that, Wright stated he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

    Wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar.

    Industry observers note that “I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my organization and the industry more than the customer,” Wright remarked. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”.

    In a recent development, tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

    That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

    “Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright said.

    According to recent reports, NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in Fresh York. Nickels mentioned that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

    It has been revealed that “The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels noted. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”.

    Some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states right now have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

    While traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to newly introduced grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

    “We lost a major incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels said.

    Breaking: The House has a latest lame-duck challenge: Attendance

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that house Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S.
    • Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a upcoming challenge: Attendance.
    • Industry observers note that thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that house Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, said attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a upcoming challenge: Attendance.

    Industry observers note that thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-reveals – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

    The House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

    "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members.".

    “We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

    In a recent development, of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-indicates; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

    Johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

    It has been revealed that “I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, mentioned. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”.

    And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

    According to recent reports, “There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

    Industry observers note that “I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”.

    Recent findings suggest that attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

    While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

    Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

    However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

    According to recent reports, “The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., said. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”.

In other words, you could use it to pay virtually nothing for a $300 hotel stay. All-in-all, I’d say the Capital One Venture bonus is worth up to $1,575.

    According to recent reports, by my valuation, the current Capital One Venture Card bonus is the best publicly available offer that we’ve seen in over five years, so that makes this the ideal time to apply, and I absolutely wouldn’t wait for a better offer.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera.
    • Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its significant-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox.
    • Jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago.

    Sources indicate that donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera. The lack of news is not just because of a (predictable) blackout enforced by the Chinese Communist Party, but because the collective consciousness of America has shut down for the next few days. If you thought the traditional four-day Thanksgiving Day Weekend was typically slow, get ready for a one-and-a-half-week productivity dip in the economy as the video game Grand Theft Auto VI goes live across the nation. Even National Review, as sober-minded as it is, has more than a few fans of the series on its staff.

    Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its significant-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox. For all I know we’ll be publishing one too. But I am not a gamer — not in the modern sense of the word, although I did whip out my copy of Battletoads for the NES the other day to prove that I’ve still “got it” — and this will not be a review of GTA VI. Instead, I want to talk about time spent — and time wasted.

    Jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago. He is also the co-host of National Review’s Political Beats podcast, which explores the great music of the modern era with guests from the political world happy to find something non-political to talk about.

    On “Grand Theft Auto VI and How We Spend Our Time”.

    Industry News: Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December.
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.
    • Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a recent development, rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    In a statement McIver mentioned she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver stated in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    Sources indicate that separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    It has been revealed that ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    In a recent development, court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    Earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of Newly introduced Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

    American Airlines Will Displace Philadelphia Pilots—Blames Union For Rejecting A321XLR Staffing Deal

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines states a “significant number” of Philadelphia pilots will be displaced from their current positions after their union’s board rejected a deal on staffing Airbus A321XLR flights to Europe.
    • That can change which trips pilots fly, the schedules they can hold, and potentially their commutes.
    • Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the company’s message to pilots:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines states a “significant number” of Philadelphia pilots will be displaced from their current positions after their union’s board rejected a deal on staffing Airbus A321XLR flights to Europe. The airline is reopening a domestic Airbus pilot base and shrinking its international one for June 2027. That can change which trips pilots fly, the schedules they can hold, and potentially their commutes. American is blaming the union for rejecting what it calls an “objectively better path forward.” Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the tech giant’s message to pilots: When we publish our June 2027 vacancy announcement tomorrow, you will see that we are reopening a PHL A320 Domestic base (Section 17.S.1) and reducing the PHL A320 International base. This will, unfortunately, result in the displacement of a significant number of pilots from the PHL A320 International base (Section 17.D). The airline says it had agreed to a term sheet with the Allied Pilots Association, completed the contractual language, and expected a signed side agreement. The union’s board rejected it November 6. November 22, 2026 The dispute connects two things that don’t seem related at first blush: which pilots get lucrative extra trips, and how American makes sure its newly introduced Europe flights have qualified crews. I wrote in April about American’s new Aggressive Pick-up system. It gives pilots access to last-minute open trips on a first-come, first-served basis. Those trips can come with premium pay. Junior pilots gained access to flying that senior pilots had been accustomed to getting. That helps American cover flights and creates opportunities for junior pilots. It also takes income opportunities away from senior ones. The fight over “fixing” the system is largely about who gets the money. The union wanted seniority to count in those awards, along with priority for pilots based where the trip originates and fixes to message delays. American saw something it could trade for. The union’s September 18 negotiating update described the exchange: Pilots would get changes to the extra-trip pickup system. Seniority and in-base priority would play a role, and the parties would address problems with how trip opportunities reached pilots. American would get changes to monthly schedule bidding for its Europe operation. The airline wanted Atlantic Europe qualifications incorporated into its Preferential Bidding System, the software that builds pilots’ schedules. The memo calls this an “A320” matter because that’s the pilot fleet category, which includes the A321XLR. A pilot qualified to fly an Airbus domestically still needs the additional qualifications for this oceanic flying. “AE” means Atlantic Europe here. American needs the pilots qualified for those trips to be available to fly them. A large pool of Airbus pilots doesn’t solve the problem if the pilots who can fly to Europe are awarded domestic schedules, while pilots who haven’t completed the necessary training are entitled by seniority to the Europe trips. The union’s October 27 update explained limited changes to bidding rules for Airbus pilots in categories with current or future XLR Europe flying, paired with seniority protections in the qualification training initiative. Pilots discussing the proposed agreement described the risk of qualified pilots being directed toward Europe trips or reserve assignments they wouldn’t otherwise choose, while unqualified pilots could lose access to trips their seniority would otherwise let them bid. Pilots across the airline could benefit from changes to extra-trip awards, while the scheduling concessions would fall on the Airbus pilots affected by Europe flying. And restoring seniority in those awards helps senior pilots at the expense of junior pilots who’ve been quick enough to claim the trips. There’s a distributional problem inside the union. Some pilots argued that the union was giving up too much: American needed flexibility for an important expansion, and the union should obtain more for it in broader contract negotiations. The union had also filed a grievance over American’s failure to implement the Line Check Pilot program from the 2023 agreement, so training capacity was already a point of contention. American’s response is to divide the Philadelphia Airbus pilot group. It will reopen a domestic category and reduce the international category. A smaller, separately staffed international group gives American a more manageable pool to qualify and schedule for Europe. That avoids needing the rejected changes to keep the existing group together. The airline is using the base and displacement provisions in its contract. Under the pilot contract, reductions in a bidding category generally displace the least senior pilots, with provisions for more senior pilots to volunteer. Displaced pilots exercise their seniority into other positions, which can set off further displacement. A pilot can remain in Philadelphia on the same aircraft family but have access to different trips and schedules. Others’ choices could mean changing bases, aircraft, or commuting arrangements. American’s 2027 Europe intends include Philadelphia–Porto beginning March 28 and Philadelphia–Vienna beginning May 6, both using the A321XLR. I toured the aircraft before it entered service. It has just 155 seats: 20 business class suites, 12 premium economy seats, and 123 in coach. American can offer a premium product across the Atlantic with fewer seats to fill than on a Boeing 787. That opens up routes and seasons where a larger aircraft is harder to justify. I liked the operational benefit of making last-minute trips available to pilots willing to fly them. Getting an airplane out on time has value, and senior pilots losing priority for some extra income standing in the way of operational reliability has been a key cause of Delta’s operational meltdowns. Management calls the rejected deal objectively better. That depends on whose schedule and income you’re counting. A senior pilot seeking premium trips and a Philadelphia Airbus pilot facing restrictions on monthly bidding are different pilots gaining benefits and incurring costs. Much of a union’s role is trading off the same or better total benefits between its members, rather than getting the best possible overall deal from the employer. And union politics play an important role, especially as the American Airlines pilots union remains in the midst of drama over whether it will stay independent or join the larger Air Line Pilots Association.
