    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Three women were escorted off an American Airlines flight from Knoxville to Charlotte on Saturday night after an argument with a flight attendant, costing passengers their connections.
    • Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident.
    • Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Three women were escorted off an American Airlines flight from Knoxville to Charlotte on Saturday night after an argument with a flight attendant, costing passengers their connections. Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident. The plane was already late getting to Knoxville, before the women could have held it up. Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026 In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. The flight attendant told the women they were ready to depart and to fasten their seat belts. The exchange escalated: The three got loud and the attendant wasn’t having it. They gone. Video demonstrates two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson indicates three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte. Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. Last year I wrote about an American Airlines passenger who told a flight attendant to shut up during the safety demonstration and wound up getting the plane sent back to the gate. It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m. Charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night. However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip. The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument. (HT: @bags) Topics on this pageAir travelAmerican AirlinesAmerican Eagle OutfittersBombardierBombardier CRJ900CharlotteKnoxvillePSA Airlines+6 more More From View from the Wing.

    Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident. The plane was already late getting to Knoxville, before the women could have held it up.

    Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026.

    In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. The flight attendant told the women they were ready to depart and to fasten their seat belts. The exchange escalated:.

    Recent findings suggest that the three got loud and the attendant wasn’t having it. They gone.

    Video demonstrates two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson claims three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte.

    Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. Last year I wrote about an American Airlines passenger who told a flight attendant to shut up during the safety demonstration and wound up getting the plane sent back to the gate.

    It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m.

    In a recent development, charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night.

    However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip.

    The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument.

    American Airlines Loses O’Hare Gate Appeal—But United’s Initiative To Drive It Out Of Chicago Is Failing

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, american Airlines just lost its appeal to undo Chicago O’Hare’s gate reshuffle.
    • The latest ruling upholds the refusal to issue a preliminary injunction.
    • Sources indicate that I still think American has the better argument about the contract.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, american Airlines just lost its appeal to undo Chicago O’Hare’s gate reshuffle. But it’s already bought two gates from Spirit, earned back gate space through its own growth, and survived United’s effort to push it out of Chicago. The airline’s position is stronger than when it sued, and judges haven’t finally decided whether the city broke its contract. The latest ruling upholds the refusal to matter a preliminary injunction. The question of whether Chicago took American’s gates too early, after promising to give the airline a chance to grow into additional space first still hasn’t been resolved. I still think American has the better argument about the contract. I’ve also been skeptical from the beginning that they’d get an injunction, since money damages seemed possible. The November 19 appellate decision fits that distinction, although the trial judge’s preliminary reading of the contract was unfavorable to American. The judge accepted that Chicago made American an explicit promise The dispute goes back to the 2018 airport lease. United was getting gates freed up by Delta’s move to Terminal 5. American objected to widening United’s advantage, and Chicago agreed to three additional gates on the north side of the L concourse extension. The lease called for gate assignments following an attached map, with those assignments remaining in place for at least twelve months. American’s argument was that it needed to actually receive the promised capacity before that protected period could run. Otherwise United could grow using its additional gates while American waited for its own, and then the city would use the unequal flying to take gates away from American. The way gates work at Chicago O’Hare is that prior flying determines future gate space (or, technically, ‘linear frontage’). That’s the problem I identified when American first filed its lawsuit. The timing was part of the bargain that got American to support the redevelopment agreement in the first place. And the trial judget accepted that the city and American had agreed to tie the process to the three additional gates becoming operational: For purposes of this motion, that much—the Court has no doubt—was the deal. His position, though, is that the city’s fingers were crossed, suggesting that the explicit written commitment didn’t make it into the final lease, or at least that American couldn’t establish that it had: The language identifies completion of the Terminal 5 expansion and an airline’s relocation there as the triggers. It doesn’t separately name completion of American’s three gates. The additional gates appear on the map as common use space, which the city controls, rather than space reserved for American’s preferential use. The lease indicates it’s the complete agreement. The judge treated its language as unambiguous and excluded the earlier negotiations as a way to add a condition to it. American’s last additional gate became operational March 14, 2025. Under its reading, the protected year therefore ran through March 2026, and the next redetermination could begin April 1, 2027. Chicago instead treated the protected period as having begun in December 2023, allowing redistribution in 2025. The city’s reading is silly. The map is part of the signed agreement. Requiring the city to deliver the capacity shown there before starting a year of protected assignments doesn’t require inventing a promise outside the contract. And designating a gate common use doesn’t explain how a gate that isn’t operational can fulfill a promise intended to let an airline ramp up flying. Why American lost the injunction appeal The appellate court assumed American could satisfy the initial requirements for an injunction and still concluded that the harm from blocking the gate changes justified denying one. It was reviewing whether the trial judge abused his discretion, NOT deciding the contract dispute from scratch. American’s problem was that it didn’t establish losing the gates would destroy its Chicago hub. It planned to operate the same number of flights using fewer gates, with more flying at less attractive times and less room to recover from delays. That could cost money, make operations worse and harm passengers but it made the injury look measurable. That was my original point – that this would be a case for future damages rather than an injunction. Meanwhile, the other airlines had planned schedules around the redistribution. United projected more than 2,000 cancellations if it were blocked. That number was overblown but the court accepted that changing the arrangements would disrupt passengers, other airlines, and airport construction. And the expectation that American would win gates back in the next allocation (which it did) undercut the argument that it faced an irreversible decline. Timing hurt American, too. Chicago announced the redistribution in February 2025. American sued in May but didn’t request preliminary relief until July. By the September hearing, the October gate changes were imminent and preparations were well underway. American argued that the city shouldn’t get to invoke the hardships from correcting an agreement they deliberately broke. The appeals court rejected that approach because it saw a reasonable dispute over what the contract meant. In my view, Chicago (intentionally) muddied the contract issue enough to make it less clear. This decision doesn’t end American’s lawsuit. It upholds the denial of a preliminary injunction. The contract claims and potential damages are still unresolved. The court rejected the argument that implementation of the gate changes had made the appeal moot, since a court could still order an effective remedy. United’s strategy ran into the airport’s actual capacity Chicago seemed strongly inclined to help its hometown airline. United’s headquarters are valuable to the city, especially with rumors of a move to Denver hanging over the relationship. My coverage of the gate dispute even generated an angry phone call from Chicago “shadow mayor” Jason Lee. United saw a chance to turn American’s slow recovery from the pandemic into a permanent retreat. American had retired too many aircraft and couldn’t rebuild everywhere at once. Fewer Chicago departures meant fewer gates, which could make future growth harder. United CEO Scott Kirby tried to create pressure by talking up American’s Chicago losses and getting financial analysts to question why it should stay. United then announced additional flying on the morning of American’s earnings call, practically writing the questions for them. This was strategic flying. United clearly didn’t want all of that additional capacity. It wanted invesors to believe that any growth would be matched, so American couldn’t improve its gate position and would just lose more money trying. Kirby told analysts United would add “as many flights as are required” to protect its gate count. Then the Federal Aviation Administration intervened. The airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines were filing, especially with construction constraining movement on the ground. Its summer order capped scheduled arrivals and departures at 2,708 per day from May 17 through October 24. The government used approved summer 2025 schedules as its baseline. It rejected rewarding airlines for filing unrealistic 2026 schedules to improve their negotiating position. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff. The cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution. The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United. American needs Chicago to rebuild the business Kirby claims American loses so much money in Chicago that it should leave. Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its aims to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months. United then revealed additional flying on the morning of American’s earnings call, practically writing the questions for them.

    This was strategic flying. United clearly didn’t want all of that additional capacity. It wanted invesors to believe that any growth would be matched, so American couldn’t improve its gate position and would just lose more money trying. Kirby told analysts United would add “as many flights as are required” to protect its gate count.

    Then the Federal Aviation Administration intervened. The airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines were filing, especially with construction constraining movement on the ground. Its summer order capped scheduled arrivals and departures at 2,708 per day from May 17 through October 24.

    The government used approved summer 2025 schedules as its baseline. It rejected rewarding airlines for filing unrealistic 2026 schedules to improve their negotiating position. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff.

    It has been revealed that the cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution.

    The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United.

    Kirby claims American loses so much money in Chicago that it should leave. Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its plans to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months.     #100207. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (940 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    It’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller remarked.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide stated.

    King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    Industry observers note that the relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will enhancement the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling mentioned.

    In a recent development, the bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    Breaking: American Airlines Passenger Admits Taking Business Class Pillows—The Airline Calls It A Favorite Confession

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5495 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, an American Airlines passenger confessed to taking home two pillows from international business class.
    • That’s a very different reaction from United Airlines, which told flight attendants to stop passengers from taking its Polaris bedding.
    • It has been revealed that we have to admit… this may be one of our favorite confessions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, an American Airlines passenger confessed to taking home two pillows from international business class. Their husband sleeps with one every night and can’t sleep without it. The second pillow is a backup. American told them it was delighted the pillows had found a loving home. That’s a very different reaction from United Airlines, which told flight attendants to stop passengers from taking its Polaris bedding. And I think American has the right instinct here. A passenger is still talking about how much they love the airline’s business class product a year after the flight. This is also an unusually good advertisement for an airline pillow. We have to admit… this may be one of our favorite confessions. We’re glad those pillows found such a loving home, and even happier to hear they’re still helping you both get a great night’s sleep! Thank you for sharing the laugh and for choosing to fly with us. — americanair (@AmericanAir) November 20, 2026 I Have Airline Blankets On My Couch On my couch at home I have American Airlines blankets from before the US Airways merger, along with Etihad first class blankets. The Etihad ones are some of the softest, most comfortable blankets I’ve ever used. They remind me of those flights, and make me want to get back on board. About a year ago, at American’s event introducing its Airbus A321XLR, I took home a 100th anniversary pillow. (With permission.) When my daughter was in preschool, parents sent their kids with sleep sacks for nap time. I sent her with a United Polaris cooling gel pillow. United actually sent me a cooling gel pillow in a promotional package in 2018. They understood the value of getting the product into someone’s home when it was their public relations team doing the sending. So it was even more odd to see passengers spending thousands of dollars with them as scoflaws. An airline can buy advertising to tell me its business class bed is comfortable. A blanket I actually use at home lets me experience a little of that comfort again. An unusual souvenir also gives someone a reason to ask about a trip. Now I’m telling the story of the flight, remembering what I liked about it, and introducing somebody else to the product. United Wanted Its Pillows Back. Holiday Inn Gave Away More Towels. In 2017, United told flight attendants to watch for passengers taking its new Saks Fifth Avenue bedding. all pillows and blankets are to be left on the aircraft at the end of each flight, including the cooling gel memory foam pillow. United noted even a few missing items per flight could add up to millions of dollars across its network. They laundered and reused the bedding over multiple flights. The same instructions allowed passengers to take amenity kits, slippers and pajamas where offered. I argued that United should see the marketing opportunity. They’d finally developed bedding that customers actively wanted to bring home! There ought to be a way to take advantage of that enthusiasm. Holiday Inn did. Back in 2003, I wrote about its towel amnesty. The IHG brand declared August 28 Towel Amnesty Day and forgave guests who’d taken towels over the years. They didn’t just promise not to chase anyone. Their original announcement included more than 60,000 souvenir towels to give away, plus a dollar for Give Kids The World for every towel story collected. They turned missing inventory into stories about people’s stays. In 2013, Hyatt actively encouraged guests to take its bath amenities. Those little bottles could remind you of the hotel the next time you used them. That meant the toiletries supplied in your room, not clearing out a housekeeping cart. And it doesn’t translate into permission to remove today’s large communal shampoo dispensers. What a shame those germ farms are. Some Of The Best Airline Souvenirs Are Meant To Leave Airlines already know that small objects can become a reason to remember them, talk about them, and even book them again. KLM’s Delft houses. The airline gives miniature Dutch buildings filled with Dutch gin to intercontinental business class passengers. They’ve been doing it since the 1950s, and release a new house each year on their October 7 anniversary. There’s even an app to track your collection. The airline has given you something to collect on a future trip. Lufthansa’s rubber ducks. These began in the bathrooms of the Frankfurt First Class Terminal in 2004. Lufthansa’s own anniversary history describes delighted guests taking them home. The airline embraced it and created special editions. A little bath toy became a recognizable part of an expensive first class experience. Delta’s trading cards. You can ask a pilot for one. Delta notes it distributed more than 3 million in 2024 and produced over 5 million for its 2025 collection. This works in coach, too. The souvenir comes with a conversation with a pilot. Other airlines offer these now, too. Virgin Atlantic’s salt and pepper shakers. The little aircraft-shaped shakers famously carry the words “pinched from” and “Virgin Atlantic” underneath. The airline has joked publicly about passengers taking them. They’ve made the souvenir story part of the design, although I’d still ask before pocketing tableware. Virgin Australia had a particularly good version of this: its business class salt and pepper shakers fit together to make the Sydney Opera House. Passengers took them home. A generic salt shaker doesn’t give you much to talk about. A tiny Opera House does. Amenity Kits Are A Marketing Deal, Too An amenity kit is supposed to go home with you. The toothbrush and eye mask help during the flight. A useful bag can stay in your life for years. I’ve written about the economics of these partnerships, including United’s Brooks Brothers kits. The brand supplying the toiletries or putting its name on the bag can be subsidizing the airline’s cost. That may mean free or discounted products, shared costs, or payments for exposure to premium passengers. In other arrangements the airline pays for a luxury name. The skincare manufacturer gets its product into the hands of someone who might buy it again. The airline gets a more desirable amenity and an association with the brand. Taking the samples home and finishing them is part of the point. Where I’d Draw The Line For passengers, the starting point is what you’re being given. Amenity kits and their contents, pajamas and personal slippers where offered, children’s activity kits, and souvenirs handed out by the airline are generally yours to keep. Bedding, mattress pads, reusable noise cancelling headphones, glasses, dishes and metal cutlery are generally equipment for use during the flight. Ask before taking them. For the airline, I’d be generous with a small, distinctive item that a passenger loves, provided it’s inexpensive enough to give away and there’s enough stock to keep delivering the promised product. Give employees room to say yes. There are clear limits. Hotel guests taking televisions is absurd. I’ve covered hotels reporting stolen mattresses. I’d ask for the pillow, take the amenity kit, and happily accept a commemorative gift like American’s anniversary cushion. If the airline wants its bedding back, selling it is another way to let the passenger keep the memory. United’s own shop lists a Saks Fifth Avenue duvet for $34 (right now out of stock, with more due November 27).     all pillows and blankets are to be left on the aircraft at the end of each flight, including the cooling gel memory foam pillow.

    United mentioned even a few missing items per flight could add up to millions of dollars across its network. They laundered and reused the bedding over multiple flights. The same instructions allowed passengers to take amenity kits, slippers and pajamas where offered.

    According to recent reports, I argued that United should see the marketing opportunity. They’d finally developed bedding that customers actively wanted to bring home! There ought to be a way to take advantage of that enthusiasm.

    In a recent development, holiday Inn did. Back in 2003, I wrote about its towel amnesty. The IHG brand declared August 28 Towel Amnesty Day and forgave guests who’d taken towels over the years.

    They didn’t just promise not to chase anyone. Their original announcement included more than 60,000 souvenir towels to give away, plus a dollar for Give Kids The World for every towel story collected. They turned missing inventory into stories about people’s stays.

    It has been revealed that in 2013, Hyatt actively encouraged guests to take its bath amenities. Those little bottles could remind you of the hotel the next time you used them. That meant the toiletries supplied in your room, not clearing out a housekeeping cart. And it doesn’t translate into permission to remove today’s large communal shampoo dispensers. What a shame those germ farms are.

    Airlines already know that small objects can become a reason to remember them, talk about them, and even book them again. KLM’s Delft houses. The airline gives miniature Dutch buildings filled with Dutch gin to intercontinental business class passengers. They’ve been doing it since the 1950s, and release a fresh house each year on their October 7 anniversary. There’s even an app to track your collection. The airline has given you something to collect on a future trip. Lufthansa’s rubber ducks. These began in the bathrooms of the Frankfurt First Class Terminal in 2004. Lufthansa’s own anniversary history describes delighted guests taking them home. The airline embraced it and created special editions. A little bath toy became a recognizable part of an expensive first class experience. Delta’s trading cards. You can ask a pilot for one. Delta says it distributed more than 3 million in 2024 and produced over 5 million for its 2025 collection. This works in coach, too. The souvenir comes with a conversation with a pilot. Other airlines offer these now, too. Virgin Atlantic’s salt and pepper shakers. The little aircraft-shaped shakers famously carry the words “pinched from” and “Virgin Atlantic” underneath. The airline has joked publicly about passengers taking them. They’ve made the souvenir story part of the design, although I’d still ask before pocketing tableware. Virgin Australia had a particularly good version of this: its business class salt and pepper shakers fit together to make the Sydney Opera House. Passengers took them home. A generic salt shaker doesn’t give you much to talk about. A tiny Opera House does. Amenity Kits Are A Marketing Deal, Too An amenity kit is supposed to go home with you. The toothbrush and eye mask help during the flight. A useful bag can stay in your life for years. I’ve written about the economics of these partnerships, including United’s Brooks Brothers kits. The brand supplying the toiletries or putting its name on the bag can be subsidizing the airline’s cost. That may mean free or discounted products, shared costs, or payments for exposure to premium passengers. In other arrangements the airline pays for a luxury name. The skincare firm gets its product into the hands of someone who might buy it again. The airline gets a more desirable amenity and an association with the brand. Taking the samples home and finishing them is part of the point. Where I’d Draw The Line For passengers, the starting point is what you’re being given. Amenity kits and their contents, pajamas and personal slippers where offered, children’s activity kits, and souvenirs handed out by the airline are generally yours to keep. Bedding, mattress pads, reusable noise cancelling headphones, glasses, dishes and metal cutlery are generally equipment for use during the flight. Ask before taking them. For the airline, I’d be generous with a small, distinctive item that a passenger loves, provided it’s inexpensive enough to give away and there’s enough stock to keep delivering the promised product. Give employees room to say yes. There are clear limits. Hotel guests taking televisions is absurd. I’ve covered hotels reporting stolen mattresses. I’d ask for the pillow, take the amenity kit, and happily accept a commemorative gift like American’s anniversary cushion. If the airline wants its bedding back, selling it is another way to let the passenger keep the memory.     #100205. Latest Update: Three Routes to VPP Revenue for Installers, EPCs, and Developers Utility programs, wholesale markets, and bilateral contracts each come with different eligibility rules, payment structures, and commercial responsibilities.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (584 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Solarpowerworldonline ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Three Routes to VPP Revenue for Installers, EPCs, and Developers Utility programs, wholesale markets, and bilateral contracts each come with different eligibility rules, payment structures, and commercial responsibilities.

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In June 2026, Google and Voltus confirmed a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM.
    • Industry observers note that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs.
    • Utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

    In June 2026, Google and Voltus confirmed a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

    Industry observers note that the deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

    Utility programs and procurement.

    Utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

    Sources indicate that beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

    Aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

    According to recent reports, while Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

    Wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

    Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

    Bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

    The appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (210 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (210 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T.
    • Recent findings suggest that the “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules.
    • Industry observers note that dave Yost is senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation at Alliance Defending Freedom.

    Senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T. Elliot Gaiser to the federal district court in Texas, preferring a favorite-son candidate whom President Trump did not nominate. But the Constitution is clear: The nomination belongs to the president, not the distinguished senator. The constitutional power to “advise and consent” does not belong to a single senator, but to the Senate as a whole. Senator Cornyn’s use of a long-standing privilege conveyed by his colleagues usurps the power of both the president and the Senate.

    Recent findings suggest that the “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules. It is a practice of the Judiciary Committee not to advance a judicial nominee to a vote without the approval of both of the State’s senators. Invented in 1916, its scope and application are entirely within the discretion of the Senate Judiciary chairman, Chuck Grassley. He ought to use his discretion to put Gaiser’s nomination to a vote.

    Industry observers note that dave Yost is senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation at Alliance Defending Freedom. He previously served as the attorney general of Ohio.

    On “Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees”.

    Etihad Debuts U.S. Credit Cards With Elite Status—But Most Americans Should Skip Them

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • credit cards, including a $499 card that offers Gold status after a single Etihad purchase.
    • Recent findings suggest that qatar Airways status that comes the first year with their premium card can get you into American Airlines and Alaska Airlines lounges on domestic trips (and American Airlines international business class lounge access).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    Etihad has launched two U.S. credit cards, including a $499 card that offers Gold status after a single Etihad purchase. That’s the sort of benefit that usually gets my attention. But I wouldn’t recommend either card to most U.S. consumers.

    Recent findings suggest that qatar Airways status that comes the first year with their premium card can get you into American Airlines and Alaska Airlines lounges on domestic trips (and American Airlines international business class lounge access). Emirates status lets you book first class awards that non-status members can’t. Etihad’s status doesn’t do either of those things, and you can earn their miles faster with other cards.

    The two cards launched November 20 through First National Bank of Omaha. They’re Etihad’s first U.S. cobrands, with annual fees of $99 and $499.

    Recent findings suggest that here are the main differences in the offers: Benefit   Etihad Guest Visa Signature   Etihad Guest Premier Visa Signature Annual fee   $99   $499 Initial bonus   40,000 miles: 10,000 after first purchase, plus 30,000 after $3,000 in spending within the first three billing cycles   60,000 miles: 20,000 after first purchase, plus 40,000 after $7,000 in spending within the first three billing cycles Etihad purchases   3 miles per dollar   5 miles per dollar Partner airline purchases   2 miles per dollar   3 miles per dollar Other purchases outside the U.S. 2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other U.S. purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar The initial offers require applying by February 3, 2027. Both cards waive foreign transaction fees. The Premier card also includes Priority Pass, a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee credit every four years, and 3,000 miles after the first Etihad purchase and at each card anniversary. The status rules are: $99 card: Silver after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days. Keep Silver with $20,000 in annual card spending or $3,000 in Etihad purchases. $499 card: Silver at account opening, then Gold after your first Etihad purchase within 90 days. Keep Gold with $40,000 in annual card spending or $8,000 in Etihad purchases. Otherwise, you get Silver. Both earn one tier mile per dollar spent. The cheaper card caps this at 25,000 tier miles per calendar year, while Premier has no cap. These are status credits, separate from the miles you redeem for travel. So you can spend towards Etihad status. I like bonusing non-U.S. purchases, but if that’s meaningful to you then the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card is far better since it earns unlimited 3 points for every $1 spent on eligible foreign transactions. And I value Alaska’s miles far more than Etihad’s. But Etihad Gold Isn’t Qatar Gold When Qatar Airways launched its U.S. cards, the premium card’s first year of Gold status was immediately useful even to someone who never planned to fly Qatar. Qatar Gold is oneworld Sapphire. That means lounge access when flying American Airlines and Alaska Airlines, including domestic trips. It even gets you into American’s business class Flagship lounges on an eligible same-day itinerary. Etihad isn’t in an alliance. Their airline partnerships don’t turn Etihad Gold into an Admirals Club membership or give you those oneworld benefits on domestic American flights. The Premier card’s Priority Pass membership is a big nothingburger. Priority Pass is a drug on the market. Everyone offers Priority Pass. And Emirates gave its credit cards a purpose when it restricted first class awards to elite members. You need Silver status or higher to book a first class Classic Reward. You don’t need an Etihad card’s status just to redeem miles for the award you want. Etihad status can help when you actually fly Etihad, especially in coach. Lounge access and other benefits depend on your tier. But someone who mainly redeems miles for premium cabins already gets many of the things status would otherwise provide with their ticket. I’d Earn The Miles With A Different Card You don’t need an Etihad credit card to earn Etihad miles. Capital One, for instance, transfers to Etihad Guest at 1:1, and Venture and Venture X earn two miles per dollar on ordinary purchases. Citi and Bilt also offer transfers to Etihad. Put $40,000 of unbonused spend on the Etihad Premier card and earn 40,000 redeemable Etihad miles, while satisfying the spending requirement to keep Gold. Put that same spending on Venture X and earn 80,000 Capital One miles, which can become 80,000 Etihad miles. Or you can transfer them to a different airline. This is why I separate a card’s initial bonus and benefits from whether it’s worth using for spending. An Etihad bonus might help someone finish off an account for a specific award. That doesn’t make the card a good place to put their continuing spend. The narrow case I’d consider is someone who regularly buys Etihad coach tickets, will use the status benefits, and can retain Gold through $8,000 of Etihad purchases rather than diverting $40,000 of ordinary spending. For someone who wants Etihad miles for an occasional business or first class redemption, I’d earn transferable points with a better card. I wouldn’t pay $499 and give up half my everyday mileage earning just for Etihad Gold. The narrow case I’d consider is someone who regularly buys Etihad coach tickets, will use the status benefits, and can retain Gold through $8,000 of Etihad purchases rather than diverting $40,000 of ordinary spending. For someone who wants Etihad miles for an occasional business or first class redemption, I’d earn transferable points with a better card. I wouldn’t pay $499 and give up half my everyday mileage earning just for Etihad Gold.     #100202. Breaking: House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1334 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1334 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, indicates banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the fresh year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, indicates banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the fresh year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    In a recent development, “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” remarked Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    Sources indicate that the incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner remarked, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the latest Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    It has been revealed that “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    Recent findings suggest that folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the matter while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    Colorado Rep. Jason Crow remarked moving forward swiftly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    It has been revealed that “I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly noted the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    Industry observers note that “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he said at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    Industry observers note that some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she said of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    According to recent reports, “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal noted. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    It has been revealed that it’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a fresh stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    Recent findings suggest that “My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and reveals right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander said.

    Sources indicate that while momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    In a recent development, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., noted Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he mentioned. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    According to recent reports, that proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley noted that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Citi AAdvantage Executive Card Review: Better Lounges And More Status Credit

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 55 min read (11086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~55 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • According to recent reports, the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] costs $695 a year, but I think it’s a better value today than it was at $595.
    • For a regular American Airlines flyer who wants Admirals Club access, it’s the place to start.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    According to recent reports, the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] costs $695 a year, but I think it’s a better value today than it was at $595. American Airlines is investing seriously in its clubs again, and the card’s refresh added more credit towards elite status and benefits I can actually use.

    I have the card. For a regular American Airlines flyer who wants Admirals Club access, it’s the place to start. The lounges are getting better, more are coming, and buying membership directly from American costs hundreds of dollars more.

    In a recent development, when I covered the refresh, I thought the additional Loyalty Points alone justified the $100 annual fee increase for me. Citi has since added $200 in annual inKind dining credits, too.

    The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® includes full Admirals Club membership for the primary cardmember. American has priced standalone membership to make getting the card the obvious choice for someone eligible to apply. Here’s the current comparison: Option   Annual Cost   What You Get Citi AAdvantage Executive card   $695   Full membership, including guest privileges and eligible partner lounges Full membership bought from American   $1,200–$1,400, depending on status   Full membership, including guest privileges and eligible partner lounges Single membership bought from American   $750   Admirals Club access for the member, without guests or partner lounges Even an Executive Platinum member pays $1,200 for full membership. The card saves $505 before assigning any value to its miles, status bonuses or credits. Someone without status saves $705. And the card costs less than American’s restricted $750 membership option. There’s no annual visit allowance to ration and no spending requirement to unlock unlimited visits. Qualifying Citigold customers can receive a $145 annual relationship credit, reducing their cost further. What The Lounge Access Includes American has nearly 50 Admirals Clubs, with more than 60 partner lounges extending the membership’s reach. Under American’s access rules: You can visit Admirals Clubs on eligible same-day itineraries, including American Airlines and oneworld flights. You don’t have to buy the ticket with this card. You can bring two guests or your immediate family—a spouse or domestic partner and children under 18. Guests need eligible same-day boarding passes, too. The primary cardmember’s membership includes eligible partner locations, such as Alaska Lounges and Qantas Clubs. The flight requirements vary by partner. This doesn’t include Flagship Lounges or Flagship Dining. Executive Platinum status by itself doesn’t get you into Admirals Clubs on ordinary domestic trips. Neither does a typical domestic first class ticket. The card also has an unusually good deal for additional cardholders: $175 total for up to three authorized people, then $175 for each additional user. Use all three slots and that’s about $58 per person annually. Each authorized user can visit Admirals Clubs without you and bring their own eligible guests. They need their physical card, identification and an eligible same-day boarding pass. They get Admirals Club access, rather than full membership, so they don’t get the partner lounge benefit. For a family, $870 in total annual fees can cover a primary cardmember and three authorized users traveling separately, with guest privileges. That’s less than American charges one Executive Platinum member for standalone full membership. If you only want a few visits a year, the $350 annual fee Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] includes four annual Admirals Club passes. American Is Finally Building Clubs I Want To Spend Time In For years American underinvested in lounges. They closed clubs, and when they renovated others the result was often the institutional look I’ve called “modern hospital.” The newer design is a huge improvement. Washington National’s E concourse club, Denver, Newark and Philadelphia show where American is going: warmer wood, better lighting, comfortable seating and spaces that feel inviting. I like this aesthetic more than the newer United Clubs or Delta Sky Clubs. The food has improved, too. I still generally prefer Delta’s lounge food, but American has moved well beyond the old snacks-and-soup proposition. Their fall Admirals Club menus include beef barbacoa taco bars in Chicago, Denver and St. Louis; sesame orange chicken at several West Coast clubs and Phoenix; and Creole style chicken with white bean cassoulet at the Upcoming York and Newark clubs. I’ve covered American’s initiative for a new, renovated or expanded lounge nearly every month, on average, over two to three years. That’s very different from what we saw for much of the past decade. Among the projects: Charlotte: A new Admirals Club exceeding 40,000 square feet, with showers and multiple bars and food stations. Dallas–Fort Worth: A 37,000 square foot Terminal C club, plus a Provisions location planned for Terminal F. Austin: A replacement club exceeding 12,000 square feet, with American’s first outdoor lounge terrace. Chicago, Nashville, Miami and Washington National: New or expanded clubs, including Chicago’s L concourse project and the refresh of National’s Concourse D club. There’s also the Provisions grab-and-go concept, already operating in Charlotte, with additional locations confirmed for New York JFK and Dallas–Fort Worth. Sometimes you want food to take to the gate more than you want a seat in a lounge. And the most valuable part of a club can still be its agents. I’ve written about the Austin agents who keep looking for better connections after I’ve left. Having someone help fix a disrupted trip can be worth more than everything you eat and drink in the lounge that year. The Initial Bonus And Who Can Get It The current public initial bonus is 80,000 AAdvantage miles after $8,000 in purchases within the first three months of account opening. The annual fee is $695. Those are redeemable miles. The initial bonus doesn’t count as Loyalty Points towards status, although eligible spending to earn it does. Under Citi’s terms, you aren’t eligible for the initial bonus if you’ve received an Executive card new account bonus within the past 48 months. The restriction also covers converting another Citi card into an Executive account when that other account earned a new account bonus within the last 48 months. Simply having a different AAdvantage cobrand card doesn’t disqualify you. Up To 40,000 Extra Loyalty Points Without Spending On The Card The card awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds during the AAdvantage qualification year, which runs March through February: Account Reaches   Cumulative Executive Card Bonuses 50,000 Loyalty Points   10,000 Loyalty Points 90,000 Loyalty Points   20,000 Loyalty Points 165,000 Loyalty Points   30,000 Loyalty Points 240,000 Loyalty Points   40,000 Loyalty Points The last two bonuses were added in the refresh. You don’t have to earn the qualifying Loyalty Points by spending on this card. Flying, shopping portal earnings, hotel bookings and spending on other AAdvantage cards can get you there. The bonuses themselves count towards subsequent thresholds. Earn 80,000 Loyalty Points outside this benefit and the first two bonuses bring you to 100,000. For someone pursuing Executive Platinum, the card can supply 30,000 of the required 200,000 Loyalty Points. Earning 170,000 elsewhere gets you there. The fourth bonus comes after Executive Platinum, helping towards higher Loyalty Point Rewards: 210,000 earned elsewhere plus the four bonuses gets you to 250,000. This is why the Executive card can make sense alongside another AAdvantage card. I have the Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], too, and its spending can help trigger these Executive card bonuses. Globe’s Flight Streak bonuses can also stack with them. The Credits That Help Pay For The Card The October inKind addition is especially useful to me. I already use inKind at restaurants I’d eat at anyway. Here’s how the recurring credits work: $200 inKind dining credit: $100 for January–June and $100 for July–December. Add the card and benefit in the inKind app, then apply the credit when paying a participating restaurant through the app. There’s no minimum spend, and you can use it across multiple checks. Unused credit doesn’t carry over. Tips aren’t covered, and authorized users share the account’s allocation. Up to $500 American Airlines Vacations credit: Up to $250 in each half of the calendar year. This covers eligible vacation packages and Experiences purchased through American Airlines Vacations. Packages require at least two travel components, such as a flight and hotel or flight and car. Up to $100 for inflight and eligible Admirals Club purchases: A calendar year statement credit for eligible purchases charged to the card. Club food and beverages qualify. The inflight benefit applies to eligible domestic American Airlines and American Eagle flights. I won’t value this at the full $100 because many of the drinks and snacks I’d otherwise buy are already included through my status or seat, but it can cover additional purchases for family or premium club drinks. Up to $120 for Avis and Budget: Each calendar year, for eligible prepaid rentals booked directly at avis.com or budget.com and charged to the card. Pay later reservations and bookings through other travel sites don’t qualify. Up to $180 in Lyft credits: Take three eligible rides paid with the card in a calendar month, then receive a $15 Lyft credit. The credit expires after 30 days. This improved from $10 to $15 per month, but three rides are still required. Starting February 1, 2027, Wait & Save rides won’t qualify. If inKind saves you $200 on dining you’d otherwise pay for, that leaves $495 of annual fee to justify with lounge access, status bonuses and the other benefits. One old benefit is being phased out: the $10 Grubhub credit per monthly billing statement. Accounts opened before August 23, 2026 retain it through August 31, 2027. New applicants don’t get it, and the old 25% inflight food and beverage rebate has ended (replaced by the annual $100 credit). Hotel, Rental Car And Airport Benefits The refresh also added Omni Champion status and the ability to earn an annual free night. Enroll in the status benefit before your stay, allowing up to 14 days for activation. Then complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights, booked directly with Omni in your name and paid with the Executive card. That earns 100 Omni Credits for a free night on a later stay, once per calendar year. Redeem within 12 months. Taxes and resort fees are included in the award. A two-night stay you were going to make anyway can produce a valuable additional night. You can also enroll in Avis President’s Club through August 31, 2028. This offers upgrades and other rental benefits, although it’s duplicative for members who already receive it by reaching 100,000 AAdvantage Loyalty Points. Other benefits include: First checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. You don’t have to pay for the tickets with the card. Priority check-in, priority security where available and Group 4 boarding for the primary cardmember and up to eight companions on the same reservation. Up to $120 towards Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years when you pay the application fee with the card. No foreign transaction fees and travel protections including trip cancellation and interruption, trip delay, lost baggage and rental car coverage for qualifying purchases. What I’d Actually Spend On The Card The earning rates are: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings. 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1 mile per dollar on other eligible purchases. Eligible spending earns one Loyalty Point per dollar. The category bonuses don’t multiply that: a dollar of American Airlines spending earns four redeemable miles and one Loyalty Point from the card. AAdvantage Hotels can separately award miles and Loyalty Points for the booking itself. The 12-mile rate is a strong reason to use this card when booking through American’s hotel and rental car platforms. I’d also use it where payment is required to earn a credit or benefit. For everyday spending, the decision is how much the additional Loyalty Points help you. American lets card spending make a real contribution to status, but earning one redeemable mile per dollar means giving up the rewards another card would have earned. You can keep the Executive card for its clubs and milestone bonuses while putting spending on a different card. After $150,000 in purchases during a calendar year, eligible American Airlines purchases earn five miles per dollar for the rest of that year. I wouldn’t do that just to earn one additional mile per dollar on subsequent airfare.
